transcript.text: Hi! I'm your AI interviewer. We'll do a quick backend round: a short intro, your experience, one coding problem, some CS fundamentals, and a couple of behavioral questions. Ready?
Hi! Yes, I'm ready. Thanks for doing this.
Great. Walk me through your background and the project you're most proud of.

I'm a final-year CS student. My biggest project is a URL shortener with Redis caching — it handles about 2k requests per second on a single instance. I designed the schema and the rate limiter myself.
Nice — 2k rps on one box is solid. What was the hardest bug you hit while building the rate limiter?
Race conditions on the token bucket. Two requests would read the same count and both pass. I fixed it with a Lua script so the check-and-decrement is atomic.

Atomic Lua — good instinct. Let's code. Problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. The editor is locked until you explain your approach.

I'll use a hash map. One pass: for each number, check if target minus the number is already in the map. If yes, return both indices; otherwise store the number with its index. That's O(n) time and O(n) space.
That's the optimal approach — clean O(n). Editor unlocked. Code it up.
Done — submitted. All 8 tests passed, including the duplicate-values case I was worried about.
8/8, well done. Quick fundamentals: what happens, at the OS level, when you call `read()` on an empty pipe with no writers?
I believe read returns 0 immediately — end of file — because there are no writers left. If there were writers, it would block.
Exactly right. Last one — behavioral: tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate on a technical decision.

My teammate wanted to add MongoDB for analytics on the shortener; I argued Postgres with a JSONB column was enough and one less system to operate. We benchmarked both, Postgres won, and we shipped faster.
Data over opinions — love it. That's a wrap! Your report is ready below.
